claim: 3229 villagers (1689 male) were included in this study.
source: 3229 villagers (1689 male) were included in this study.
evidence: Direct statement of study population size and gender distribution from the manuscript.

claim: During the study period, 80 study participants were diagnosed with clinical P. falciparum.
source: During the study period, 80 study participants were diagnosed with clinical P. falciparum.
evidence: Direct statement of clinical diagnosis count from study data.

claim: 201 participants were found to have P. falciparum by uPCR.
source: 201 participants were found to have P. falciparum by uPCR.
evidence: Direct statement of uPCR-detected infection count from study data.

claim: 325 uPCR-positive participants had Plasmodium infections not identifiable at the species level and thus were not included in these analyses.
source: 325 uPCR-positive participants had Plasmodium infections not identifiable at the species level and thus were not included in these analyses.
evidence: Direct statement about excluded participants from the analysis.

claim: After MDA, the vast majority of clinical P. falciparum episodes occurred in only one of the study villages (TOT).
source: After MDA, the vast majority of clinical P. falciparum episodes occurred in only one of the study villages (TOT).
evidence: Direct statement about spatial distribution of clinical episodes post-MDA.

claim: 66 out of the 80 participants who had a clinical P. falciparum episode were from TOT village (three from HKT, seven from TPN and four from KNH).
source: 66 out of the 80 participants who had a clinical P. falciparum episode were from TOT village (three from HKT, seven from TPN and four from KNH).
evidence: Direct statement providing breakdown of clinical episodes by village.

claim: 19 of the 80 (24%) participants who had a clinical episode were found to have a uPCR-detected P. falciparum infection in at least one of the surveys.
source: 19 of the 80 (24%) participants who had a clinical episode were found to have a uPCR-detected P. falciparum infection in at least one of the surveys.
evidence: Direct statement about overlap between clinical and subclinical infections.

claim: uPCR-detected P. falciparum infections were more prevalent in males than females (UOR: 2.03; CI: 1.50–2.76).
source: uPCR-detected P. falciparum infections were more prevalent in males than females (UOR: 2.03; CI: 1.50–2.76).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical analysis showing gender difference in infection prevalence.

claim: uPCR-detected P. falciparum infections were widespread in all villages at baseline.
source: uPCR-detected P. falciparum infections were widespread in all villages at baseline (Figure 2).
evidence: Statement supported by Figure 2 showing spatial distribution of infections at baseline.

claim: uPCR-detected P. falciparum infections were significantly reduced following MDA in all villages.
source: These infections were significantly reduced following MDA in all villages.
evidence: Direct statement about the effect of MDA on infection prevalence.

claim: The prevalence of uPCR-detected P. falciparum infections had reduced in two control villages (villages TPN and HKT) prior to MDA.
source: The prevalence of uPCR-detected P. falciparum infections had reduced in two control villages (villages TPN and HKT) prior to MDA.
evidence: Direct statement about temporal trends in control villages.

claim: There were statistically significant clusters of uPCR-detected P. falciparum infections in each village at baseline but subsequently no significant clusters were detected.
source: There were statistically significant clusters of uPCR-detected P. falciparum infections in each village at baseline but subsequently no significant clusters were detected (Figure 2).
evidence: Statement based on spatial cluster analysis (SaTScan) shown in Figure 2.

claim: Clusters of clinical P. falciparum episodes occurred in two villages (KNH and TOT).
source: Clusters of clinical P. falciparum episodes occurred in two villages (KNH and TOT).
evidence: Direct statement about spatial clustering of clinical episodes.

claim: The cluster in KNH occurred from M5 through M7 but included only four episodes.
source: The cluster in KNH occurred from M5 through M7 but included only four episodes.
evidence: Direct statement about temporal and quantitative characteristics of KNH cluster.

claim: A cluster in the western portion of village TOT began in M12 and lasted until M18 with a total of 35 episodes.
source: A cluster in the western portion of the village began in M12 and lasted until M18 (with a total of 35 episodes).
evidence: Direct statement about spatial, temporal, and quantitative characteristics of TOT cluster.

claim: A single-house cluster occurred in the eastern portion of village TOT (M15 through M18) with five episodes among four house members.
source: A single-house cluster occurred in the eastern portion of the village (M15 through M18) with five episodes among four house members (2 in a 10 yo male, 1 in a 48 yo male, 1 in a 16 yo male, and 1 in a 48-year-old female).
evidence: Direct statement with detailed demographic information about household cluster.

claim: There were significant clusters of non-participation in the MDAs in three of the study villages (TPN, HKT and TOT).
source: There were significant clusters of non-participation in the MDAs in three of the study villages (TPN, HKT and TOT (Appendix 1—figure 2)).
evidence: Statement based on spatial cluster analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The non-participation cluster in TOT made up a large portion of the western part of the village and included 115 individuals not participating in the MDA (out of 919 total individuals in TOT).
source: The non-participation cluster in TOT made up a large portion of the western part of the village and included 115 individuals not participating in the MDA (out of 919 total individuals in TOT).
evidence: Direct statement about spatial and quantitative characteristics of non-participation cluster.

claim: The non-participation clusters in HKT and TPN included 206 and 15 individuals respectively.
source: The non-participation clusters in HKT and TPN included 206 and 15 individuals respectively.
evidence: Direct statement about size of non-participation clusters in two villages.

claim: Sporadic clinical P. falciparum episodes occurred in village TOT following MDA (MDA was completed by M3), followed by a small outbreak beginning in M12.
source: Sporadic clinical P. falciparum episodes occurred in village TOT following MDA (MDA was completed by M3), followed by a small outbreak beginning in M12 (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: Statement about temporal pattern of clinical episodes supported by Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The first clinical P. falciparum episodes during the outbreak in TOT occurred among villagers who lived in the cluster of non-MDA participation.
source: The first clinical P. falciparum episodes during this outbreak occurred among villagers who lived in the cluster of non-MDA participation (Figure 3).
evidence: Statement about spatial relationship between outbreak origin and non-participation cluster, supported by Figure 3.

claim: By M15 the clinical episodes in TOT were occurring through much of the village.
source: By M15 the clinical episodes were occurring through much of the village (Figure 3).
evidence: Statement about spatial spread of outbreak supported by Figure 3.

claim: 4.4% of all individuals in low MDA non-adherence neighborhoods had at least one clinical P. falciparum episode by the end of the study period, in comparison to 7.6% in mid and 9.6% in high MDA non-adherence neighborhoods (log-rank test p-value=0.0485).
source: 4.4% of all individuals in low MDA non-adherence neighborhoods had at least one clinical P. falciparum episode by the end of the study period, in comparison to 7.6% in mid and 9.6% in high MDA non-adherence neighborhoods (log-rank test p-value=0.0485; Figure 4A).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test results showing relationship between neighborhood adherence and clinical episodes, supported by Figure 4A.

claim: After MDA, clinical P. falciparum episodes in village TOT were most likely to occur among 5 to 14 year olds (AOR: 3.41; CI: 1.33–8.77, compared to 0 to 4 year olds).
source: After MDA, clinical P. falciparum episodes in village TOT were most likely to occur among 5 to 14 year olds (AOR: 3.41; CI: 1.33–8.77, compared to 0 to 4 year olds) and participants who lived in a house with someone else who had a clinical P. falciparum episode during the same month (AOR: 3.43; CI: 1.52–7.72), after adjusting for other covariates (Table 1).
evidence: Statement from multivariable regression analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Participants who lived in a house with someone else who had a clinical P. falciparum episode during the same month had 3.43 times the odds of having a clinical episode (AOR: 3.43; CI: 1.52–7.72).
source: After MDA, clinical P. falciparum episodes in village TOT were most likely to occur among 5 to 14 year olds (AOR: 3.41; CI: 1.33–8.77, compared to 0 to 4 year olds) and participants who lived in a house with someone else who had a clinical P. falciparum episode during the same month (AOR: 3.43; CI: 1.52–7.72), after adjusting for other covariates (Table 1).
evidence: Statement from multivariable regression analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Individuals who lived in a neighborhood with a high proportion of people who did not adhere to MDA had 2.85 times the odds of having a clinical episode (AOR: 2.85; CI: 1.28–6.37) compared to people who lived in neighborhoods where most people adhered to MDA.
source: Individuals who lived in a neighborhood with a high proportion of people who did not adhere to MDA had 2.8 times the odds of having a clinical episode (AOR: 2.85; CI: 1.28–6.37) compared to people who lived in neighborhoods where most people adhered to MDA (Table 1).
evidence: Statement from multivariable regression analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The human biting rate was associated with increased odds of having a clinical P. falciparum episode, with a 10% increase in odds for every one unit increase in HBR (AOR: 1.09; CI: 1.05–1.13).
source: The human biting rate was also associated with increased odds of having a clinical P. falciparum episode, with a 10% increase in odds for every one unit increase in HBR (AOR: 1.09; CI: 1.05–1.13).
evidence: Statement from multivariable regression analysis.

claim: The increase in clinical P. falciparum episodes in M12 coincided with an increase in HBR in village TOT.
source: The increase in clinical P. falciparum episodes in M12 also coincided with an increase in HBR in village TOT (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: Statement about temporal correlation between clinical episodes and HBR, supported by Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: Individuals from neighborhoods with low MDA adherence had 2.85 times the odds of having a malaria episode post-MDA in comparison to those from high adherence neighborhoods, regardless of individual participation.
source: In this study, individuals from neighborhoods with low MDA adherence had 2.85 times the odds of having a malaria episode post-MDA in comparison to those from high adherence neighborhoods, regardless of individual participation, suggesting a herd effect.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract summarizing key finding with statistical result.

claim: There is a herd effect from MDA for P. falciparum malaria.
source: In this study, individuals from neighborhoods with low MDA adherence had 2.85 times the odds of having a malaria episode post-MDA in comparison to those from high adherence neighborhoods, regardless of individual participation, suggesting a herd effect.
evidence: Inference drawn from the finding that neighborhood adherence affects individual risk independent of individual participation.

claim: High mosquito biting rates are predictors of clinical episodes.
source: High mosquito biting rates, living in a house with someone else with malaria, or having an asymptomatic malaria infection were also predictors of clinical episodes.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract summarizing predictors identified in the analysis.

claim: Living in a house with someone else with malaria is a predictor of clinical episodes.
source: High mosquito biting rates, living in a house with someone else with malaria, or having an asymptomatic malaria infection were also predictors of clinical episodes.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract summarizing predictors identified in the analysis.

claim: Having an asymptomatic malaria infection is a predictor of clinical episodes.
source: High mosquito biting rates, living in a house with someone else with malaria, or having an asymptomatic malaria infection were also predictors of clinical episodes.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract summarizing predictors identified in the analysis.

claim: Spatial clustering of non-adherence to MDA, even in villages with high overall participation, may frustrate elimination efforts.
source: Spatial clustering of non-adherence to MDA, even in villages with high overall participation, may frustrate elimination efforts.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract presenting a speculative conclusion based on study findings.

claim: MDA has historically been used for P. falciparum malaria.
source: MDA has historically been used for P. falciparum malaria (Poirot et al., 2013) and has recently been trialed in several locations in Africa (Gitaka et al., 2017; Mwesigwa et al., 2018; Shekalaghe et al., 2011) and Asia (Manning et al., 2018; Tripura et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2018; Pongvongsa et al., 2018; Landier et al., 2017a).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Poirot et al., 2013.

claim: MDA has recently been trialed in several locations in Africa.
source: MDA has historically been used for P. falciparum malaria (Poirot et al., 2013) and has recently been trialed in several locations in Africa (Gitaka et al., 2017; Mwesigwa et al., 2018; Shekalaghe et al., 2011) and Asia (Manning et al., 2018; Tripura et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2018; Pongvongsa et al., 2018; Landier et al., 2017a).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Gitaka et al., 2017; Mwesigwa et al., 2018; Shekalaghe et al., 2011.

claim: MDA has recently been trialed in several locations in Asia.
source: MDA has historically been used for P. falciparum malaria (Poirot et al., 2013) and has recently been trialed in several locations in Africa (Gitaka et al., 2017; Mwesigwa et al., 2018; Shekalaghe et al., 2011) and Asia (Manning et al., 2018; Tripura et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2018; Pongvongsa et al., 2018; Landier et al., 2017a).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Manning et al., 2018; Tripura et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2018; Pongvongsa et al., 2018; Landier et al., 2017a.

claim: MDA is being considered by several nations as a tool for malaria elimination.
source: It is being considered by several nations as a tool (to be used in unison with other interventions) for elimination (World Health Organization, 2017; Zuber and Takala-Harrison, 2018), and has already been implemented as an operational strategy in at least one modern setting (Parker et al., 2017; Landier et al., 2018a).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to World Health Organization, 2017; Zuber and Takala-Harrison, 2018.

claim: MDA has already been implemented as an operational strategy in at least one modern setting.
source: It is being considered by several nations as a tool (to be used in unison with other interventions) for elimination (World Health Organization, 2017; Zuber and Takala-Harrison, 2018), and has already been implemented as an operational strategy in at least one modern setting (Parker et al., 2017; Landier et al., 2018a).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Parker et al., 2017; Landier et al., 2018a.

claim: One historical malaria eradication campaign relied on the inclusion of sub-therapeutic levels of antimalarials distributed in table salt across large populations.
source: One historical malaria eradication campaign relied on the inclusion of sub-therapeutic levels of antimalarials distributed in table salt across large populations (Pinotti et al., 1955).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Pinotti et al., 1955.

claim: The table salt antimalarial program likely led to the emergence of parasite resistance in the same regions.
source: This program likely led to the emergence of parasite resistance in the same regions (Wootton et al., 2002) and this has in part led to hesitance among some institutions (i.e. the World Health Organization and ministries of health) to implement MDA for malaria (World Health Organization, 2015a).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Wootton et al., 2002.

claim: The table salt antimalarial program has in part led to hesitance among some institutions to implement MDA for malaria.
source: This program likely led to the emergence of parasite resistance in the same regions (Wootton et al., 2002) and this has in part led to hesitance among some institutions (i.e. the World Health Organization and ministries of health) to implement MDA for malaria (World Health Organization, 2015a).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2015a and inference from historical context.

claim: MDA can quickly reduce or eliminate parasite reservoirs and can act as a catalyst for subregional elimination of P. falciparum malaria.
source: Used appropriately, MDA can quickly reduce or eliminate parasite reservoirs and can act as a catalyst for subregional elimination of P. falciparum malaria (Landier et al., 2018a).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Landier et al., 2018a.

claim: Some literature has suggested that at least 80% coverage and adherence of MDA in the targeted population is necessary in order for the MDA to be successful.
source: Some literature has suggested that at least 80% coverage and adherence of MDA in the targeted population is necessary in order for the MDA to be successful (World Health Organization, 2015b).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2015b.

claim: The notion of a herd effect providing additional levels of population protection from antimalarial MDA is plausible but has not been examined empirically.
source: If the aim for antimalarial MDA is to interrupt transmission, the notion of a herd effect providing additional levels of population protection is plausible but has not been examined empirically (Cotter et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Cotter et al., 2013.

claim: This is the first documentation of a herd effect conferred by MDA for P. falciparum malaria.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first documentation of a herd effect conferred by MDA for P. falciparum malaria.
evidence: Direct statement claiming novelty of the finding.

claim: HBR peaked in village HKT at the same time as in village TOT.
source: HBR also peaked in one other village (HKT) at the same time as in village TOT (Appendix 1—figure 3), but occurred in the absence of a detectable parasite reservoir and the HBR did not persist at high levels.
evidence: Statement about temporal pattern in HBR supported by Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: The HBR peak in HKT occurred in the absence of a detectable parasite reservoir and the HBR did not persist at high levels.
source: HBR also peaked in one other village (HKT) at the same time as in village TOT (Appendix 1—figure 3), but occurred in the absence of a detectable parasite reservoir and the HBR did not persist at high levels.
evidence: Statement comparing HBR patterns between villages supported by Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: Evidence suggests that the malaria post in TOT was not functioning well in the first year of the study.
source: Evidence also suggests that the MP in TOT was not functioning well in the first year of the study (reported in Landier et al., 2017a).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Landier et al., 2017a.

claim: The combination of a persisting parasite reservoir and persistently high HBR (from M13 – M18) in TOT likely explains the drastically different results between the study villages with regard to P. falciparum malaria elimination.
source: The combination of a persisting parasite reservoir and persistently high HBR (from M13 – M18) in TOT likely explains the drastically different results between the study villages with regard to P. falciparum malaria elimination (Figure 2).
evidence: Inference drawn from observed patterns in parasite reservoir and HBR data.

claim: A better functioning malaria post in TOT would likely have reduced the size of the outbreak.
source: A better functioning MP in TOT would likely have reduced the size of the outbreak.
evidence: Speculative statement based on inference about the role of the malaria post.

claim: Interventions such as reactive case detection would have resulted in the detection of extra cases when searching within houses and occasionally in neighboring houses.
source: This clustering suggests that interventions such as reactive case detection would have resulted in the detection of extra cases (of both clinical and uPCR-detected P. falciparum) when searching within houses and occasionally in neighboring houses, but these would have only been a small proportion of all infections within the villages (Parker et al., 2016) and would not have halted transmission.
evidence: Inference about potential effectiveness of reactive case detection based on observed clustering patterns, with citation to Parker et al., 2016.

claim: Reactive case detection would have only detected a small proportion of all infections within the villages and would not have halted transmission.
source: This clustering suggests that interventions such as reactive case detection would have resulted in the detection of extra cases (of both clinical and uPCR-detected P. falciparum) when searching within houses and occasionally in neighboring houses, but these would have only been a small proportion of all infections within the villages (Parker et al., 2016) and would not have halted transmission.
evidence: Inference about limitations of reactive case detection based on observed clustering patterns, with citation to Parker et al., 2016.

claim: Community based early diagnosis and treatment and MDA with high participation, targeted at the village scale or larger, appear effective at reducing prevalence, incidence, and transmission of P. falciparum.
source: Conversely, community based early diagnosis and treatment and MDA with high participation, targeted at the village scale or larger, appear effective at reducing prevalence, incidence, and transmission of P. falciparum (Landier et al., 2018b).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Landier et al., 2018b.

claim: Individuals who did not participate in MDA also did not participate in blood screenings immediately after MDA.
source: Individuals who did not participate in MDA also did not participate in blood screenings immediately after MDA (i.e. M3 in village TOT).
evidence: Direct statement about participation patterns in the study.

claim: uPCR-detected infections are likely to be underdiagnosed for individuals who did not participate in MDA.
source: uPCR-detected infections are therefore likely to be underdiagnosed for these individuals, and it is likely that such infections clustered and overlapped with the clusters of non-adherence to MDA.
evidence: Inference about potential bias in infection detection based on participation patterns.

claim: Underdiagnosed infections likely clustered and overlapped with the clusters of non-adherence to MDA.
source: uPCR-detected infections are therefore likely to be underdiagnosed for these individuals, and it is likely that such infections clustered and overlapped with the clusters of non-adherence to MDA.
evidence: Inference about spatial relationship between underdiagnosed infections and non-adherence.

claim: It is likely that underdiagnosed infections, combined with the high HBR, led to a resurgence of clinical episodes in TOT.
source: While no genetic analyses were done with samples from the village, it is likely that these underdiagnosed infections, combined with the high HBR, led to a resurgence of clinical episodes.
evidence: Inference about causal mechanism for outbreak resurgence.

claim: There is evidence of a poorly functioning malaria post in village TOT, which could have led to undiagnosed clinical episodes, especially during the beginning of the study.
source: There is also evidence of a poorly functioning MP in this village, which could have led to undiagnosed clinical episodes, especially during the beginning of the study.
evidence: Statement about potential limitation in case detection.

claim: Some infections are likely to be acquired outside of the village, leading to complex spatial patterns in infections that are mapped at the house level.
source: Some infections are likely to be acquired outside of the village, leading to complex spatial patterns in infections that are mapped at the house level.
evidence: Statement about potential limitation in spatial analysis due to imported infections.

claim: Within-household clustering can be the result of within-household transmission, or shared exposure outside of the household or village among household members.
source: Within-household clustering can be the result of within-household transmission, or shared exposure outside of the household or village among household members.
evidence: Statement about potential mechanisms for observed household clustering.

claim: Clinical episodes decreased among all groups for a longer period than the prophylactic effect (approximately 1 month) of the administered antimalarials.
source: First, clinical episodes decreased among all groups for a longer period than the prophylactic effect (approximately 1 month) of the administered antimalarials.
evidence: Statement presenting evidence for herd effect based on temporal patterns.

claim: There was a lag of approximately 1 month between the onset of clinical episodes in neighborhoods with mid and low MDA adherence and then occurred in neighborhoods with high MDA adherence.
source: Once the P. falciparum outbreak began (M12), there was a lag of approximately 1 month between the onset of clinical episodes in neighborhoods with mid and low MDA adherence and then occurred in neighborhoods with high MDA adherence (Figure 4A).
evidence: Statement about temporal pattern in outbreak spread supported by Figure 4A.

claim: Neighborhoods with high MDA adherence never experienced the same levels of infection as those with mid or low MDA adherence.
source: Second, neighborhoods with high MDA adherence never experienced the same levels of infection as those with mid or low MDA adherence (Figure 4A).
evidence: Statement presenting evidence for herd effect based on infection levels, supported by Figure 4A.

claim: Individuals who participated in MDA but lived in a neighborhood with low adherence had the highest risk of having a clinical episode.
source: Individuals who participated in MDA but lived in a neighborhood with low adherence had the highest risk of having a clinical episode whereas those who did not participate in MDA but lived in a neighborhood with high adherence had the lowest risk of having a clinical P. falciparum episode (Figure 4B).
evidence: Statement about risk patterns supported by Figure 4B.

claim: Individuals who did not participate in MDA but lived in a neighborhood with high adherence had the lowest risk of having a clinical P. falciparum episode.
source: Individuals who participated in MDA but lived in a neighborhood with low adherence had the highest risk of having a clinical episode whereas those who did not participate in MDA but lived in a neighborhood with high adherence had the lowest risk of having a clinical P. falciparum episode (Figure 4B).
evidence: Statement about risk patterns supported by Figure 4B.

claim: The individual-level finding that non-participants in high adherence neighborhoods had low risk may be related to relative perceptions of risk, with potential complacency among individuals living in areas with lower levels of malaria.
source: As has been described in other settings, this individual-level finding may be related to relative perceptions of risk; with potential complacency among individuals living in areas with lower levels of malaria (Koenker et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference about behavioral mechanism supported by citation to Koenker et al., 2013.

claim: Living in a neighborhood with a high proportion of people who did not adhere to MDA was a significant risk factor for acquiring a clinical P. falciparum episode, after adjusting for individual MDA adherence and other important predictors.
source: Third, the results from the multivariable logistic regression also suggest that living in a neighborhood with a high proportion of people who did not adhere to MDA was a significant risk factor for acquiring a clinical P. falciparum episode, after adjusting for individual MDA adherence and other important predictors of having a clinical episode (Table 1).
evidence: Statement presenting evidence for herd effect from multivariable analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The study site consisted of four villages (KNH, TPN, HKT, and TOT) along the Myanmar-Thailand border, in Kayin (Karen) State, Myanmar.
source: The study site consisted of four villages (KNH, TPN, HKT, and TOT) along the Myanmar-Thailand border, in Kayin (Karen) State, Myanmar (Landier et al., 2017b).
evidence: Direct statement about study location with citation to Landier et al., 2017b.

claim: The villages were selected based on P. falciparum malaria prevalence surveys using ultrasensitive quantitative PCR (uPCR).
source: The villages were selected based on P. falciparum malaria prevalence surveys using ultrasensitive quantitative PCR (uPCR) (Imwong et al., 2015) and were part of a MDA pilot study (Landier et al., 2017b).
evidence: Direct statement about village selection criteria with citations to Imwong et al., 2015 and Landier et al., 2017b.

claim: The northernmost village is approximately 105 km from the southernmost village.
source: The northernmost village is approximately 105 km from the southernmost and the two closest villages, KNH and TPN are within 10 km of each other (Figure 1).
evidence: Direct statement about geographic distances supported by Figure 1.

claim: The two closest villages, KNH and TPN, are within 10 km of each other.
source: The northernmost village is approximately 105 km from the southernmost and the two closest villages, KNH and TPN are within 10 km of each other (Figure 1).
evidence: Direct statement about geographic distances supported by Figure 1.

claim: The study was conducted from May 2013 through June 2015.
source: The study was conducted from May 2013 through June 2015.
evidence: Direct statement about study duration.

claim: A full population census was completed in each of the four study villages at baseline May – June 2013.
source: A full population census was completed in each of the four study villages at baseline May – June 2013.
evidence: Direct statement about census data collection.

claim: Everyone enumerated in the census was given a unique identification code.
source: Everyone enumerated in the census was given a unique identification code.
evidence: Direct statement about data management procedures.

claim: Geographic coordinates were collected for all houses in the four study villages.
source: Geographic coordinates were collected for all houses in the four study villages and a unique identification code was assigned to each house.
evidence: Direct statement about spatial data collection.

claim: Blood surveys were conducted at baseline in each village, aiming to screen all individuals above an age of 9 months.
source: Blood surveys were conducted at baseline in each village, aiming to screen all individuals above an age of 9 months.
evidence: Direct statement about blood survey procedures.

claim: Venous blood (3 mL) was drawn from each participant and analyzed using a highly sensitive quantitative PCR (uPCR) assay with a limit of detection of 22 parasites per mL.
source: Venous blood (3 mL) was drawn from each participant, transported to a central laboratory and analyzed using a highly sensitive quantitative PCR (uPCR) assay with a limit of detection of 22 parasites per mL. (Imwong et al., 2014).
evidence: Direct statement about laboratory methods with citation to Imwong et al., 2014.

claim: Most (86%) uPCR-detected infections were subclinical.
source: Most (86%) uPCR-detected infections were subclinical (Landier et al., 2017a) and clinical infections were provided the standard treatment (see below).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to Landier et al., 2017a.

claim: A community-based malaria clinic was established in each village at the beginning of the project, as part of the malaria intervention.
source: A community-based malaria clinic (referred to as a malaria post or MP) was established in each village at the beginning of the project, as part of the malaria intervention.
evidence: Direct statement about intervention implementation.

claim: Village health workers were trained to diagnose malaria using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and to treat RDT positive infections with dose based on weight and age.
source: Village health workers were trained to diagnose malaria using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and to treat RDT positive infections with dose based on weight and age.
evidence: Direct statement about training and treatment protocols.

claim: Malaria episodes were treated with dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHA + P) for P. falciparum and chloroquine for P. vivax.
source: Malaria episodes were treated with dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHA + P) for P. falciparum and chloroquine for P. vivax.
evidence: Direct statement about treatment protocols.

claim: Radical cure for P. vivax was not provided because the absence of G6PD tests required to prevent hemolysis in G6PD individuals.
source: Radical cure for P. vivax was not provided because the absence of G6PD (Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) tests required to prevent hemolysis in G6PD individuals (Bancone et al., 2014; Chu et al., 2017).
evidence: Direct statement about treatment limitations with citations to Bancone et al., 2014; Chu et al., 2017.

claim: MDAs were conducted in two villages at the beginning of the study (month 0, M0) and extended to the two control villages beginning in month 9 (M9).
source: MDAs were conducted in two villages at the beginning of the study (month 0, M0) and extended to the two control villages beginning in month 9 (M9).
evidence: Direct statement about MDA timing.

claim: Restricted randomization was used to decide which villages received early or deferred MDA.
source: Restricted randomization was used to decide which villages received early or deferred MDA.
evidence: Direct statement about study design.

claim: MDA consisted of 3 days of DHA + P, with a single low dose of primaquine on the third day, repeated over three months.
source: MDA consisted of 3 days of DHA + P, with a single low dose of primaquine on the third day, repeated over three months (M0, M1, M2 for the first group and M9, M10, M11 for the control group).
evidence: Direct statement about MDA regimen.

claim: Follow-up blood surveys were conducted in each village every third month after M0 until M18.
source: Follow-up blood surveys were conducted in each village every third month after M0 until M18.
evidence: Direct statement about follow-up survey schedule.

claim: A final full blood survey was completed in each village at M24.
source: A final full blood survey was completed in each village at M24.
evidence: Direct statement about final survey timing.

claim: Mosquitoes were collected monthly using human landing catches to estimate the human biting rate (HBR).
source: Mosquitoes were collected monthly using human landing catches to estimate the human biting rate (HBR).
evidence: Direct statement about entomological data collection methods.

claim: Mosquito catching teams were based at five sites (both indoors and outdoors) within each of the four study villages for five consecutive nights during the study period M0 through M20.
source: Mosquito catching teams were based at five sites (both indoors and outdoors) within each of the four study villages (total of 20 catch sites) for five consecutive nights during the study period M0 through M20.
